newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian inflation fight may be hard - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian inflation fight may be hard - analysts.

text.p: Analysts are split over the question of whether Hungary will be able to slash inflation as quickly as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) proposed.

But most analysts say that the government, if it wants to cut inflation in 1998 quicker than the originally-planned five percentage points, will have to reach a wide social consensus on a sharp decrease in the pace of wage and price rises next year.
"A social and economic agreement should be reached (for a substantial cut in 1998 inflation)," said Peter Bozso, analyst of OTP Securities. "But this is very difficult to carry out.
Hungary plans to reduce inflation to 17-19 percent in 1997 from 23.6 percent last year, and to cut it by at least a further five percentage points in 1998.

Finance Ministry officials, urged by the IMF to make a radical cut, said recently that the 1998 budget draft, already being prepared, may include a larger reduction and could even target single-figure inflation.
The ministry said price movements were already almost fully liberalised and the state of the economy did not justify high inflation, now running at 19 percent year-on-year.

A drastic cut in inflation would substantially decrease the interest payments on state debt, enabling the government to cut expenditure and lower rates, thus revving up the economy, the ministry said.
The main stumbling block in the way of this ambitious plan is what both analysts and politicians refer to as "the psychological factor".

Hungarians have lived with high inflation rates for the past few years and, after a more than 15 percent slump in real wages in the past two years, it would be hard to convince them to risk another large decline in real wages, analysts said.
"People have got used to galloping wages," said Judit Barta, analyst of GKI Research Institute.
The Socialist-Liberal government would also be in a difficult position if it wanted to curb wage rises ahead of the 1998 elections, analysts added.

"The prospect (of the elections) would be heavily felt during wage negotiations," said ING Barings analyst Douglas Reid. "I think (a radical inflation cut) would be difficult as wage pressure becomes an important factor, but not totally impossible."

The two ruling parties' popularity is at an all-time low and well below that of opposition parties following a decline in living standards and a recent privatisation -- and alleged corruption -- scandal.
"I am an economist but I do not think the political background (of a price and wage agreement) is secured," said Barta.
However, Prime Minister Gyula Horn told a news conference on Monday he did not believe that an agreement on wages could be the most important factor to influence inflation.
He said that there was a chance for inflation to go down to between nine and 13 percent in 1998 as he did not see large price increase in the next two years.
All analysts agree that Hungary's inflation will steadily decline in the next two years and many say that the economy is ripe for low inflation.

But other analysts said that necessary and costly structural changes, such as the reform of the social security, were likely to slow the decline of inflation and recreate inflationary pressures later if delayed for political reasons.
